title: Why 'Get Rich' Gurus Sell Courses Instead of Doing It

spine.goal: Dave wants the guru's 'million-dollar system' so he can quit his job. He already paid $1,997 for a three-day workshop and is about to pay $9,997 for the 'Platinum' level.
spine.stakes: $9,997 on a credit card (on top of the $1,997 already gone) - more than everything Dave has saved.
spine.central_question: If the guru's system really makes a million dollars a year, why is he selling it to Dave instead of just using it?
spine.loop_big: The one question that made the guru's enrollment coach hang up on Dave (promised in o6, paid in ch8).
spine.loop_mid: Pause-and-guess (ch2, ~30%): how high did the upsell ladder go in a real FTC case? Paid at the end of ch3: $41,297 (Zurixx).
spine.villain: The course-selling funnel itself: the course IS the business. Revealed at ~50% with MOBE ($125M+ per the FTC), where 'the primary thing MOBE sells is more MOBE memberships'.
spine.low_point: ~75%: the 'risk-free' refund turns into a maze, Dave's workshop buddy Kevin is told the fix is buying the next level, and Dave is tempted to spend $9,997 to 'earn it back'.
spine.win: Dave learns what the FTC already says about earnings claims and pressure tactics, keeps proof, reports it, asks his card company about a dispute, closes the Platinum tab (SAVED $9,997) and asks the one question that ends the pitch.

sources: FTC press release, June 2018, 'FTC Action Halts MOBE, a Massive Internet Business Coaching Scheme': defendants allegedly took more than $125 million from thousands of consumers; $49 entry fee for a '21-step system', then membership packages costing thousands of dollars; the 'proven system' turned out to be selling the same memberships to others; most buyers could not recoup their costs, some lost more than $20,000; refunds often refused or paid only after persistent demands (ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2018/06/ftc-action-halts-mobe-massive-internet-business-coaching-scheme)

FTC Business Blog, June 2018, 'FTC alleges MOBE tells a whale of a tale with misleading money-making claims': 21-Step System for $49 or less; Gold Masterclass $4,997; Diamond Mastermind $29,997; FTC: 'the primary thing MOBE sells is more MOBE memberships'; fine print: 'the average Consultant ... generates less than $250 per year'; '100% risk-free' 30-day money-back promise (ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2018/06/ftc-alleges-mobe-tells-whale-tale-misleading-money-making-claims)

FTC press release, Oct 2019, 'FTC Acts Against Company Using Celebrity Endorsements, Bogus Earnings Claims to Sell Real Estate Seminars' (Zurixx, with Utah Division of Consumer Protection): free event was a sales pitch for a $1,997 three-day workshop, described as 'beginner' level; upsells cost as much as $41,297; presenters routinely told attendees to get new credit cards or raise credit limits; some refund recipients had to sign agreements barring them from speaking with the FTC (ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2019/10/ftc-acts-against-company-using-celebrity-endorsements-bogus-earnings-claims-sell-real-estate)

FTC press release, July 2024, 'FTC Sends More Than $12 Million in Refunds to Consumers Harmed by Zurixx': more than $12 million to 25,563 consumers; February 2022 settlement permanently banned the defendants from selling real estate or business coaching programs (ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/07/ftc-sends-more-12-million-refunds-consumers-harmed-zurixx-real-estate-investment-coaching-scheme)

FTC press release, 26 Oct 2021, 'FTC Puts Businesses on Notice that False Money-Making Claims Could Lead to Big Penalties': Notice of Penalty Offenses sent to more than 1,100 businesses including business coaching; listed deceptive practices include misrepresenting earnings, claiming profits are typical, claiming no experience is needed, and claiming consumers must act immediately

FTC press release, 13 Jan 2025, 'FTC Proposes Rule Changes and New Rule to Deter Deceptive Earnings Claims by Multilevel Marketers and Money-Making Opportunity Sellers': proposal (3-2 vote) to extend the Business Opportunity Rule (16 CFR 437) to money-making opportunities such as business coaching; sellers would need written substantiation for earnings claims; deceptive earnings claims are already illegal

PBS American Experience, 'The Gold Rush' (film and companion features): Sam Brannan waved a vial of gold through San Francisco shouting 'Gold! Gold from the American River!' after stocking up on prospecting supplies; sales at his store near the mines totaled $36,000 in May, June and early July 1848; he never mined, and became California's first millionaire; most miners did hard labor and many ended up as wage workers
FTC ReportFraud portal: reportfraud.ftc.gov (where consumers report money-making scams)
Illustrative math (story, not a statistic): $1,997 x 1,000 buyers = $1,997,000 in revenue for one recorded workshop. Dave, Kevin, the guru and the coach are fictional characters.

beats.text: Two A M. Dave is about to pay nine thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars.
For a course on getting rich. Yep, that's Dave. Rewind.
Three weeks earlier, a mansion guy said: I made a million last year.
The F T C says one program like this took over one hundred twenty five million dollars.
So why would a millionaire sell his secret?
Stay for the one question that made the guru hang up.
So Dave clicked. Free training. Ninety minutes. He grabbed a snack and got ready for the secret.
Minute one, the guru showed his mansion. Minute ten, his car. Minute forty, a jet ski.
Minute eighty five. Still no secret. But there was an offer. A three day workshop, for one thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars. Only twenty spots. And a timer.
It's like a free sample at the grocery store. Except the guy with the toothpick follows you all the way to the checkout.
Dave watched the spots tick down. Nineteen. Eighteen. Seventeen. He bought one.
And on day one of the workshop, Dave heard a sentence he'd hear again and again. This is just the beginner level.
Day one, Dave filled a whole notebook. Lots of excitement. Very few actual steps.
Day two, the guru explained. The real system lives in the advanced program. Gold. Platinum. Diamond.
It's like a game that's free to download. Then the sword costs money. Then the armor. Then the horse. And somehow you never reach the castle.

And this isn't a made up guru trick. The F T C sued a real estate coaching company called Zurixx. First, a free event. Then a three day workshop for one thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars. Then the upsells.
Quick guess. How high did that ladder go? What did the most expensive package cost? Write your number in the comments. The answer is in a minute.
Back at the workshop, a coach pulled Dave aside. Platinum, he said. Nine thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars. Credit limit too low? Just call your card and ask for more.
Dave had one night to decide. So he did something the guru never taught. He looked the guru up.
Dave searched the mansion photo. It was a vacation rental. You can book it by the night.
Then he searched for the guru's million dollar business. He found exactly one business. The course.
And that reminded Dave of a story from eighteen forty eight.
A shopkeeper named Sam Brannan ran through San Francisco, waving a little bottle of gold, shouting: Gold! Gold from the American River!
Thousands rushed off to dig. But Brannan had already stocked up on picks, pans and shovels. His store near the mines sold thirty six thousand dollars of goods in about two months.
Most miners got blisters. Brannan became California's first millionaire. And he never dug for gold.
Oh, and the answer to the guess. In the Zurixx case, the upsells went as high as forty one thousand two hundred ninety seven dollars. For coaching.
So Dave asked himself the scary question. What if the course isn't how the guru got rich? What if the course is the gold?
Dave went looking for the biggest case he could find. Remember that one hundred twenty five million dollars? That program was called MOBE. My Online Business Education.

It started at forty nine dollars, for a twenty one step system. Then came the masterclasses. Gold, four thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars. Diamond, twenty nine thousand nine hundred ninety seven.
And the proven system for making money? According to the F T C, it was mostly selling more of the same memberships to other people.
In the F T C's own words, the primary thing MOBE sells is more MOBE memberships.
It's like a restaurant where the only dish on the menu is a recipe for opening a restaurant.
And the fine print? The average member made less than two hundred fifty dollars a year. Some people lost more than twenty thousand.
So there's the villain. Not one guy in a mansion. The machine behind him. A sales funnel built to move you up one more step, again and again.
But that left Dave with a weird question. If someone really had a money machine, why would they sell it at all?
Dave thought about his uncle's secret fishing spot. It's full of fish. And his uncle has never told anyone where it is.
Because if he sold a map to a thousand people, the spot would be empty by Tuesday.
Real money tricks work the same way. The more people use them, the less they work. So a real secret gets kept, not sold.
But a course is a different animal. You record it once and sell it forever. No shop. No stock. No risk.
Do the math. A one thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollar workshop, sold to a thousand people, is almost two million dollars. Even if nobody in the room ever flips a single house.
Dave used to think: he's rich, so he must know the secret. Nope. He's rich because people like Dave believed he knew the secret.
So Dave decided to get his money back. That's when things got worse.
Dave emailed support. The sales page had promised: one hundred percent risk free. Thirty day money back guarantee.
Reply one. Please fill out the form. Reply two. First, you must finish every lesson. Reply three. Nothing.
It was like pushing a revolving door. Lots of effort, and you always end up right where you started.

And it's not just Dave's bad luck. The F T C says MOBE often refused refunds, or paid only after people kept demanding. In the Zurixx case, some people had to sign a paper promising not to talk to the F T C.
Then Dave's workshop buddy Kevin texted. He'd bought Platinum, on two credit cards. And his coach had the perfect fix. Buy the next level.
Dave stared at his own Platinum offer. Still open. Two spots left. Maybe he had to spend more to earn it all back?
It looked hopeless. But there's one thing these gurus really don't want you to know. And it's sitting right there in the rules.
Dave opened the F T C website. Quick reminder, this is education, not advice.

Clue one. Lying about earnings is already illegal. In twenty twenty one, the F T C warned more than eleven hundred companies, including business coaching sellers, that fake money claims could bring big penalties.
Clue two. That warning even lists the tricks. Saying the profits are typical. Saying you don't need experience. Saying you must act immediately. Dave's countdown timer suddenly looked very different.
Clue three. In twenty twenty five, the F T C proposed rules aimed right at business coaching. Any earnings claim would need written proof behind it.
So Dave made a plan. He saved screenshots of every promise. He reported the program at report fraud dot F T C dot gov. And he asked his card company about disputing the charge.
And the Platinum offer? Dave closed the tab. Nine thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars, saved.
But Dave still had one call booked with his enrollment coach. And this time, he'd prepared a question.
The coach picked up, all smiles. So, Dave. Ready for Platinum?
Dave said: maybe. One question first. What did your typical student earn last year, after paying for the program? And can you send that in writing?
Silence. Then: well, results vary. Then: oh, I have another call. Click.
That's the question. Not how much did you make. How much did your typical buyer make. In writing.
Because the guru's real number was never his income. It was how many Daves bought the course.
A guy with a real money machine doesn't need your two thousand dollars. A guy selling one does.
One. If someone sells the secret, the selling is the business.
Two. Free training is just the first step of a long ladder.
Three. Ask what the typical buyer earned. In writing.
A week later, Bob knocked on Dave's door. Not with a course. With a business opportunity. And Bob swears it's not a pyramid.
Subscribe, so the raccoon can't sell you a course on spotting raccoons.

youtube.title: Why 'Get Rich' Gurus Sell You Courses Instead of Doing It
alt_titles: You Paid $1,997 for His System. Why Is He Selling It?
Why Your 'Free Training' Always Ends With an Upsell
youtube.hook: It's 2 AM and Dave is about to pay $9,997 for a course on getting rich. If the system really works, why is the guru selling it instead of using it? Dave joins a free webinar, buys a $1,997 'beginner' workshop, and is one click away from the $9,997 Platinum level. We follow the upsell ladder step by step, using what the FTC found in real cases: one program took more than $125 million while its average member made under $250 a year, and another pushed upsells as high as $41,297. Then the 1848 gold rush shopkeeper who got rich without digging, why the refund guarantee turns into a maze, and the one question that made the sales coach hang up.
youtube.pinned: Have you ever bought a course that promised to make you rich? What happened? (No judgment, Dave almost paid $9,997.)
